utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Confirmed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, I'd like to go back briefly, and very briefly if I may, to your 2002 written statement that was given to the ICTY. In that statement, as we yesterday discussed, and I'd be happy to give it to you if you'd like, that again on the issue of reviewing numerous documents relevant to the trial of Dr. Stakic, it says "numerous documents" we talked about that yesterday. And I appreciate your answers on that. What I want to know is what the word "relevant" means, and who determined what documents, whether they were numerous or not, who determined that the documents were relevant for Dr. Stakic and his case?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If necessary, I'll call the investigator who dealt with it, but I can say straight away that the documents were given by the investigator to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's the testimony of the witness now, and not the one of the OTP. The witness may answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was shown a number of documents during the interview preceding this trial. Everything that was shown me then put in front of me from my own position it seemed relevant. I wasn't the one to select the documents from the file. The team of investigators approached me and told me: "Can you please look through these documents." I did not select them as I saw fit. These documents were just there. Why these documents are legally relevant, perhaps you and Your Honours could say. At this moment, I really don't know the legal relevance of what you've just asked me, but I respect your profession and I tried to answer your question. As far as the legal formulation and the legal relevance is concerned, I think it's quite pointless to ask me about that. I agreed to cooperate, and whatever was shown me, both here and there, is something that I can form my opinion on the basis of and in terms of my own experience, and that's all I can answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. But my question doesn't relate to the definition legally of the word "relevant." And I recognise you're not a lawyer. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You've never studied law, in any capacity. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's not right or it's correct that you never studied law in any capacity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't study law.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So I'm not asking for a legal definition of relevance. My point is as follows, if I may, sir, you don't know, since you did not select the documents, what is or is not relevant to the case of Dr. Milomir Stakic. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I looked through the documents that were shown me. If anyone asked me if there was a link, a connecting thread, between those documents, being an engineer and not a lawyer, what I could say is that the connection is the SDS, the Crisis Staff, the area, and part of that area. That's all I could say. But I don't think my own view is very helpful in this matter. Documents did relate to the problems dealt with by this Tribunal. That, I think, is obvious enough. What the relevance is in this particular case, don't ask me to be a judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. We'll move on on the issue of relevance. I take it from the statement that you signed, Miss Joanna Korner was present at that interview as well. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You don't remember, or you're not sure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I signed the statement after the interview and after I had looked through those documents. It's possible that she was there, but I'm not sure really. It was a formal issue. I just had a quick look, and I signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Briefly, how long did your process of reviewing these documents that were not selected by you, how long did it take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How long? Two or three days on several separate occasions because at a later stage, we did discuss a number of those documents. I asked questions about some of the documents, some of the documents I had no opinion on. Some I had held a view about in the earlier trials, and it's possible I said something to the effect because some of the documents had been used in the earlier trials. But I didn't see any relevance within that procedure in taking up the pen and then numbering which in a different situation I would have done, of course, the exact hours I spent working on those documents. So in the future, I may be well advised to do so, so we spare ourselves the effort and the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sejmenovic. If I may now turn to another issue, please, briefly we discussed yesterday -- I'm going to try to walk through the entire period from the elections of November 1990 up and through, and obviously there's a relevant time period subsequent to that, but up and until and through September of 1992 based on the testimony that you've provided four or so sessions here. So my first issue, or I'm going to cover two issues related to the pre-election period which is immediately prior to 1990. Sir, I don't need and necessarily want you to go back too far in history so we're limited to that period when the SDA, HDZ, and SDS formed their parties. So closer to the period of November. Is that fair? Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I will try to help and answer all the questions that I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There was an interparty agreement between the three majority parties: SDA, HDZ, and SDS, prior to the November 1990 elections. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Generally speaking at the Republic level, several talks were held between the three parties; the presidents of the parties and the top-level leaders. That was a generally known fact. There was also a general agreement that if the elections were won, a coalition government would be formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the agreement actually, to the best of your knowledge, was a coalition between which parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We're talking now about the pre-election period, and several talks were held between the leaders of the three parties. The so-called national parties, the SDS, the SDA, and the HDZ. That was a generally known fact, also published in the media and the newspapers as well as the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. electronic media.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Was this agreement, the interparty agreement between those three parties that you mentioned, was it ever reduced to writing or was it simply an oral agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't really remember whether there was anything in writing. But I know that the agreement was very firm and that principles were set down if the elections were won, how power would be distributed. I'm sure you can check this in Sarajevo. I think that's a very simple thing to check, whether there was anything in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you share with us the sum and substance of that firm agreement and those firm principles that you just described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only speak now in a very general way about the essential point of those negotiations, so the essence was once we succeeded in toppling the communists or the left-wing bloc, power would be distributed according to a very simple principle. All the national parties would partake in power, equal representation in government bodies, and then the rest depending on results at the local level. The party taking the majority of votes would get the most representatives, and then the second biggest party would get the second biggest number of representatives, and that's how these positions were to be filled. At the republic level, and also at the local level as we were instructed, to also include the opposition wherever possible and to assign to the opposition parties the lower-ranking positions wherever possible. In some places, they did manage to implement this, and in some they didn't. In Prijedor, we tried to have something like that, but we couldn't reach a more general agreement with the other parties, specifically the SDS, maybe even the HDZ but I can't remember now. That was the general platform that was later to be put in place, at least initially during the first stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it your position, sir, that the SDS violated this interparty agreement prior to the November 1990 elections?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which part of the agreement are you referring to? I have enumerated several elements of this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As to any elements that you've described for us, I would simply like to know your position whether prior to the November 1990 elections, whether or not the SDS violated any of those terms of the interparty agreement, and then if you could share with us which ones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the republic level or at the municipal level?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At both.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Prior to the elections, neither at the republic level nor at the municipal level was it possible to violate the agreement because the elections had not taken place yet, and there was no power to distribute. So, confusion arose after the elections. There were negotiations between the parties at the republic level about the distribution of the leading positions, but this didn't last for a very long time, because they were distributed quite quickly. In most of the municipalities, the process was completed without any major complications. In some of the municipalities, problems did occur later on, related to the distribution of power. Speaking of this latest stage, we can say that yes, the SDS did indeed violate the agreement. That is my view speaking from my position at that time, my position as an SDA official. And also based on what I remember we had offered the local branch of the SDS. So that's when they began to disregard this joint agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that you participated in the formation of the municipal authority or government in the Prijedor Municipality after the elections of November 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The SDA did take part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you, sir, participate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not part of the executive power. I was physically present, but I was not myself a candidate for executive power, nor did I devise any new scheme for the division of power. There was an agreement, and all the leading top positions were distributed quite quickly, but then the remaining offices -- the distribution of the remaining offices became a moot point.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So you were present but you did not participate, correct, in the participation with respect to the Prijedor government authority in the municipality. Is that a fair way to say it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was the party, sir, and there were the party organs. On the other hand, you had another party, and a third party which took part in the negotiations. Before every negotiation, proposals were to be agreed on, and after each and every one of the talks, regardless of the results, favourable or less favourable, conclusions were presented at the -- to the executive board. So, if someone was a member of the Executive Board of the party, not necessarily the president or the vice-president but this person was very well informed about what was going on, and what is participation exactly? What does that mean? Sometimes you just raise your hand. Sometimes you draw a proposal on behalf of others, and then the others may have to determine it. It's a very relative concept. If I was in the leadership of the party, there was not only one man there. There was the presidency, the Executive Board, and the municipal board. I did partake in the work of these organs, which means that I was kept well informed. But not in the sense in which you could say that I was a member of the negotiating team. And you may be right on this point because I never went to the meeting of the three officials of the SDA and the SDS where we would sit down and negotiate. I took part in no such meetings. During the negotiations about this situation, how it really was on the level of what was said, I couldn't tell. But those leaving a session of the Executive Board, I know what their duty was and what they had to come back with to the board and what they had to present. We had very simple solutions, very simple, not much philosophy is needed to understand that solution. "Gentlemen, no division of power has been implemented yet. Please, let's carve it up in two halves, if you please. We'll have the half we like or we'll just carve it up, so please have either of the two halves." It was a very simple matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So am I correct that you participated not directly, but indirectly, as a member of the republic of the Chamber of Municipalities of Prijedor and as the first vice-president of the SDA? Correct? Would that be a fair generalization?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, if you like. You can indeed define it in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it true, sir, that based on this interparty agreement, that the SDA in Prijedor selected the foremost post in the municipality, that being the president of the municipality assembly of Prijedor, Mr. Cehajic? Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the basis of a pre-electoral agreement, the SDA received the post of the president of municipality, so that was based on a pre-electoral agreement. That was something agreed with the SDS, and that was no request. It was a normal result of the -- a normal consequence of the election result for the SDA to have the president of municipality, for the SDS to have the president of the municipal government. That was never disputed because it had been agreed in the pre-election period. Should the SDS win the elections, they will have the president of the assembly. If the SDA came second, the president of the government would be an SDA member. The elections took place, and the transition occurred. The place of Marko Pavic was taken over by Muhamed Cehajic from the SDA, the president of the municipal government was Marko Kovacevic. At that stage, there were no problems really. There was a preelectoral agreement concerning this issue, and after the elections, this agreement was simply carried out. The problems arose when the remaining positions of power had to be distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I think that's why my question said "based on the interparty agreement" and that's what I'm basing it on essentially. In connection with that, you mentioned a gentleman by the name of Marko Kovacevic. Is it Milan Kovacevic or is it Marko Kovacevic who became the president of the municipal government. Just so the record is clear, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never mentioned Marko Kovacevic. I only said the late Dr. Kovacevic. And as far as Mr. Muhamed Cehajic from the SDA is concerned, he took over the position of president of municipality from Marko Pavic. The former president from the socialist system. It is quite possible that this has been misinterpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It is quite possible, and that's why on the transcript it revealed that, and that's why I just wanted to correct it so there would be no confusion. The primary post for the municipality of Prijedor in 1990 after the elections was to select and the SDA selected its member. The second most influential post was actually, as you just said, the president of the government, and that was given to the SDS, and that was to Mr. -- the late Dr. Milan Kovacevic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: There is no doubt that those two posts were the post influential posts in the entirety of the Prijedor Municipality from the elections of 1990. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you could say that these were the two most prominent positions in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And as this highest function or the most prominent positions in the municipality, can you tell us, if you know, what the duties and obligations were of the president of the Municipal Assembly, and then the president, as you call it, of the government, namely Dr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't interpret these issues legally. Of course you will understand that. But I know the essence of both of these positions. The Municipal Assembly is the highest legislative body at all. It is chaired by the president of the assembly. He also proposes the agenda and convenes the session. People used to refer to him as the president of the municipality. So that was the foremost function and the highest legislative position in a municipality. Are you ready? Because I haven't completed my answer. In addition to the legislative power and the assembly as its highest body, there was also executive power, so this is a general principle applying to all levels and to most countries in the world. The head of the executive power or municipal government, as we refer to it, was Mr. Kovacevic. His position was the president of the Executive Board. His competence was to convene sessions of the government, and the government consisted of the most prominent men from all the different sections of society, culture, economy, and so on. He was supposed to convene sessions of the government to preside over these sessions, to work towards solutions, and, in a practical sense, to virtually govern, or to propose laws or amendments to laws to the assembly after which the assembly would convene and adopt a decision, make amendments, or choose not to do so. So that was the essence of these two positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So when you say that the late Dr. Milan Kovacevic was the president of the government, he was in actuality of the president of the Executive Board of the Prijedor Municipality. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I tried to emphasise nominally it's called the president of the Executive Board, but popularly referred to as the president of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In that short period after the elections, can you tell us, the late Mr. Cehajic as president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, what influence, if any, did he have on the republic level with respect to republic institutions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Concerning the communication between the different -- between the local level and the republic institutions, occasionally at times, heads of municipality were called to meetings, to attend meetings at the republic level. I don't know which institutions called them, but I know that there were a number of such cases. I would not know about the details, but I know that, formally, heads of municipality did not compose any specific body that regularly met at the republic level, but there were invitations to meetings, so probably that came from the government level of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, from some sectors of the government. But I'm not qualified to speak about that because I simply do not know a sufficient number of facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: You, being the republic representative for the municipality of Prijedor in the Chamber of Municipalities after 1990, to whom would the republic assemblymen turn to to discuss issues which may or may not concern the Prijedor Municipality? Would they turn to the late Dr. Cehajic, or would they turn to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not quite understand the question, I believe. Whom the delegates from the republic level would go to speak to at the local level? Was that your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not quite, but that's not a bad question. But my question is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this: If there was an issue that the late Dr. Cehajic wanted to discuss that involved a republic institution, let's take the military, for instance, would he go to you first, or would he go directly to the republic assembly to have that issue resolved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, he didn't need to address the republic assembly. If the issue on the agenda involved the military at the level of the municipality, there was the secretariat for the national defence. Its command was located in Sarajevo. There could have been some intermediate stages, but the final one was in Sarajevo. If public security was the issue, then there was the ministry of the interior. If necessary, he was able to address the minister of the interior. I'm now talking to you about the normal way of proceeding. In reality, I can tell you only about how I, as a deputy, functioned within this municipality. It was my duty, my obligation, and I made it clear to everyone, publicly, at the assembly sessions and on various other occasions that if they had any problems or any initiatives, any solutions for problems, in terms of passing new legislation, then I would be conveying those to the level of the republic. And in that capacity, I sometimes had contacts to that effect with Muharem [as interpreted] Cehajic, even with the people from the SDS. So I was a deputy who was obliged to convey certain problems, but only those which required the application of the parliamentary procedure. I would have to rely on some people who would prepare that for me, and then I would bring it up at the session of the assembly, or wait for the opportune moment to do that. And that is the way that I proceeded and worked. As for the problems related to specific departments within the municipal authority, such as the police, financial affairs, the economy, the military, there was a regular structure in place. And it would have been logical for a relevant chief or the head of the department or the president of the municipality, depending on the level of the problem, to use this avenue to solve these problems. He was able to contact the minister of defence, the minister of the economy or whoever he needed to speak to, depending on the issue. That was the practice that was applied. I cannot really say that this was always followed in Prijedor. I wasn't able to observe everything. But I had a general insight into how the communication worked. And I always entertained this type of contacts, and I still do, and I believe this would have been the normal procedure in other countries as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The position or organ that you mentioned, secretariat for the national defence, was that a local, meaning Prijedor municipality, and I know you mentioned it was Sarajevo, was it at the republic level or was it at the federal level, this institution, the secretariat for national defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The secretariat for the national defence operated at the local level, but it existed also at the level of the republic. Before the elections, it had existed at the federal level as well. So what you had was the so-called SSNO, the federal secretariat for the national defence, RSNO, that is, the republic secretariat for national defence, and locally speaking, you had OSSNO, the municipal secretariat for the national defence. They are part of one and the same hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So if the late Dr. Cehajic had a problem in 1990, with respect to either a financial or economic issue or a military issue, since we talked about that specifically, would he contact the local, republic, federal, or which secretariat for the national defence would he be able to contact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he was able to contact the local level institution. And it was his duty. He was the head of the local community, generally speaking. It was his obligation to deal with the problems at the local level. If the problems were of such nature that they exceeded the local significance, then it was also possible for him to contact a higher level, that is, the level of the republic. I say that it was possible for him to contact, whether he did or didn't, I don't know unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And let me ask you: Did he have any powers, other than the power and ability to make contact with the various hierarchial divisions of the secretariat of the national defence that you described, other than to contact them and to perhaps complain about an issue that is before him? Did he have any powers whatsoever with respect to that issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I'm afraid that we do not understand each other. I wish to reiterate certain things. The most important function of the president of the Municipal Assembly was to govern the municipality. And all the spheres of public life within the municipality. He was in charge of nominating and appointing the cabinet. You asked me whether he had any connections, any contacts with the higher level of authority, and I told you, as far as I know, again, I'm not a lawyer, there was not a regular channel of communication, that is, it was not an obligation of Cehajic to submit his reports to a republic-level institution. That was not provided for. But as a head of the municipality, he had the right to present certain personal views at the assembly in Sarajevo. Whether he did that or not, I don't know, but he definitely had the right to do so. However, most often, if the problem was of a legislative nature, then he would convey that problem to the deputies, who would then have the obligation to present it to the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo, because it would be unnatural and improper for him to travel to Sarajevo and to argue a problem in front of the assembly on his own. That was our function. If a problem involved a specific department, and if the head of the department was not willing to implement a decision that had come out from the level of the republic, then it was also possible for the president of the municipality to contact both instances to see what it was all about. That was the most logical way of proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: If the president of the municipality of Prijedor, hypothetical question, after 1990, wanted to remove a military unit who was perhaps performing military exercises in the area of Prijedor, did the late Mr. Cehajic have any powers whatsoever to go to the military and to tell them to: "Please leave the territory of which I am president, namely the municipality of Prijedor?" Did he have any such powers to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that, sir. I would need to have a look at the rules of procedure and the relevant statutes and to see what the relevant competencies were to tell you whether he had that right or not. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Help me with this: You were the deputy selected as the only member on the republic level from the Chamber of Municipalities for the municipality of Prijedor. Did you, sir, have that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The authority to order a military unit to relocate? There was a legislative system in place which was very precise and clear, and which provided for specific competencies and rights and duties. Please, allow me, if you yourself are not able to do that, to try and obtain for you the relevant statutory regulations. I'm sure that they exist in various archives, and you will be able to see what it was all about. You're asking me, who is by no means an expert in these issues, to tell you what the procedure was. But as I said, I really don't know. I do not wish to make any serious mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I accept your offer, by the way, and look forward to that. But my question is this to you, sir, yourself: Did you have an competencies that you, yourself, were able to remove, order the removal and ask that a military unit, after 1990, move out of the area where you were the republic deputy representative in the Chamber of Municipalities for the municipality of Prijedor? Did you have any of those competencies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I was a deputy at the assembly of the republic, which means that I was part of a legislative body. I was not a member of any government, neither at the local nor at the republic level. I have nothing -- that is, I had nothing to do with the executive power, the one that is in charge of issuing orders and decisions. I, as a member of the legislative power, do not have any such competencies. I am now talking about my competencies as a deputy in the republic parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you identify any individual post-1990 who had competencies, whether at the legislative or the executive branch of the local level who had the right and the power to ask that a federal institution remove itself from the territory in which that local representative may have been appointed or elected? Do you know of anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as federal institutions are concerned, the only level which, according to law, had authority to discuss the issues of a federal nature was the republic level of Bosnia and Herzegovina, not any municipal level. It's perfectly logical. There was the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and if certain issues were not clear concerning the links between the municipal and the republic government, republic and federal level, they would discuss those issues. But you are now asking me about people who were sitting at the local level in the municipality. The level which we turned to was the level of the republic. A totally different issue is the fact that some of the federal institutions had very articulated departments at various lower levels, but the level of the republic was the same as the level of a federal state. While it still functioned, while there were links to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to move to a slightly different topic before we break, and I understand that the break is in about approximately 15 or so minutes. And that issue involves weapons and armaments in part. We're going to discuss it at length. I just have a couple issues regarding pre-election weapons and armaments. So is it true, sir, that prior to the election, meaning prior to November 1990, that it was decided to take almost all, indeed, to withdraw almost all of the weapons and armaments from the Territorial Defence, that is, the territorial units and to store them in a central depot in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This problem didn't concern Prijedor exclusively. Prijedor was by no means an exception. What I know was that prior to the elections, there had been a major reorganisation of the Yugoslav army, the federal army, and I know that the boundaries of the so-called military districts had been changed. I know that it was from the federal level that an order had been issued, the order that the weapons of the Territorial Defence should be withdrawn from the relevant areas and handed over to the JNA, who would then store it in their warehouses and take care of it. It was a publicly discussed issue that we could learn about from the media. Later, a large number of requests were made to that effect. Some of the were complied with. As for the time when this decision to withdraw the weapons was made, I don't know, I don't know the exact dates. But I know that the issue was topical at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you mentioned that this was a decision made at the federal level pertaining to a federal institution, namely, the JNA. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The decision concerned the Territorial Defence. You asked me about the Territorial Defence. So it was a federal decision which concerned Territorial Defence departments in republics, in the republics. And pursuant to this decision, the JNA was tasked with taking over the weapons which belonged to the Territorial Defence. That decision was implemented on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And while the reorganisation of the Yugoslav People's Army was underway, and that occurred when the Sarajevo army district was abolished. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I'm trying to find the most simple way of explaining this. The army was being reorganised, and this was written about by the media. Before that, there had been a so-called Sarajevo military district, I think, which covered the most -- the largest part of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the command was located in Sarajevo. After this reorganisation of the Yugoslav People's Army, the Sarajevo military district was abolished, and this -- the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina was divided between two different military districts, the Sarajevo -- two or three different military districts. The Sarajevo military district no longer existed, which does not mean that the military was no longer present in Sarajevo. They were still there, as it was the case with all other areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina, even to a greater extent than before. However, command was no longer exerted from Sarajevo. I'm talking about the units deployed in Bosnia and Herzegovina. These units were now being commanded from the command which was located in Podgorica in Montenegro, which was part of the new plan. This was a very contentious issue and a former generals from the partisan era were involved in this. So this particular military district was divided in several parts. One part thereof went to the Uzice Corps, I think, and the Sarajevo military district no longer existed. But the presence of the military in Sarajevo was even increased after this reorganisation. I wanted to explain this because I wanted to avoid any confusion. It is true that the military district was abolished, but the military was still Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. strongly present there. And some argued that this reorganisation actually went to the detriment of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they later on proved to be right, arguably.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to argue with you about that. All I want to know, sir, and if you can answer this question, and I truly appreciate your explanations, was it decided to take almost all, to withdraw almost all the weapons and armaments from the Territorial Defence, that is, the territorial units, and to store them in a central depot in Prijedor? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A decision was made to that effect, a decision which was later implemented. But I don't know exactly when. I don't want to speculate, but I know that it was implemented. Later, when tensions mounted, people from the relevant areas, from the ground, made such requests, that is, that the weapons be returned to the Territorial Defence which entailed a number of discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Where was the central depot in Prijedor located? Was it in the town of Prijedor, or in the general municipality also called Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know where it was. I assume it was located in one of the barracks under the control of the army, but I don't know. I've never been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I can just read from your 1996 transcript, May 23rd, 1996, specifically page 903, line 31 through 33, and then the passage immediately following on page 904 of the May 23rd, 1996 passage, because I have a couple questions on that that I'd like to cover if I can before our next break. It states on line 31: "Question: Was the TO in Prijedor armed in 1990 at the time of the elections?" "Answer: No." "Question: Where had the arms gone?" Following page, page 904: "Answer: The arms were withdrawn from territorial units, that is, from neighbourhood communities before the elections while the reorganisation of the Yugoslav People's Army was underway, when the Sarajevo army district was abolished, it was used to cover the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was decided then to take almost all the -- to withdraw almost all the weaponry and armaments from the Territorial Defence, that is, territorial units, and to store them in a central depot in Prijedor." On line 16, you do, sir, state also as you have today, that a symbolic number of pieces were returned, and we will get to that issue later. All I want to know with respect to that statement that I read now, is it correct and accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is correct. The barracks was located in Prijedor, and the weapons were the local communes were transported to the Prijedor barracks. Where they were stored, in what depots or warehouses, the question should not be addressed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Can you tell us, since you know about the territorial units to some extent, how many territorial units had the weapons been withdrawn from and placed in the central depot in Prijedor prior to 1990, November 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Prior to November 1990. Prior to that time, I did not have any insight into the workings of the army, the Territorial Defence, the municipality, or any other state organ. I was only informed on that through the media. But one thing is sure: During that period of time the Yugoslav army and the orders -- did implement the orders on the disarming of the Territorial Defence. But I cannot speak about the details of this order. I've never read it. I don't have it in front of me. But the fact remains that the weapons were transported from the local communities where they had been stored prior to that, elsewhere. Only a small number of these -- of this weapon remained. Later on, with the change of power, when we were able to inform ourselves on the work of the local communes and the Territorial Defence organisations, we were able to see, to realise, that the order had been carried out, and that the majority of these weapons had been transported. I can talk about the functioning of these organs after the elections, but not before. If I had taken part in power before the elections, maybe I wouldn't have participated in the elections, or maybe I would have been on a different side.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, all I want to know is with respect to the arms, weapons and armaments that you mention, both here today and in 1996, can you describe for us what types of weapons and armaments from the various territorial units were stored in the central depot in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, I cannot. I believe that I've already stated clearly that I was not a member of the Territorial Defence, nor was I any kind of commander at any level. How many pieces of weapons the Territorial Defence had and in which local commune these weapons were, I don't know. I know about the people who were members of the Territorial Defence who told me that the weapons had been relocated, and they also told me what kind of weapons remained. Later, when the weapons were returned, they also spoke about the kinds of weapons -- the types of weapons that were returned. So this is something that I can tell you about. However, regarding the type of weapons that the Territorial Defence had before, while the federal organs were still in place, I don't know. But I believe that it should be possible to obtain documents to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sejmenovic, for that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we break, may I ask the Defence, is there a consent, you heard before, that during the break, I will be contacted by representative of the Office of the Prosecutor? Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, she is coming to Court, so the Defence can hear what she is going to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 4.30, okay. Then we can -- then let's have the break until 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we, as time is of essence, restart with the cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, just to finish a couple more questions with respect to this central depot or barracks, as it has been identified, in the Prijedor area, can you tell us- and again, I understand you don't know prior to November 1990, but how about after November 1990, up until March of 1992, if you will, who secured the central depot in Prijedor where those weapons and armaments were held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that there was a garrison of the JNA in Prijedor. It was in the Urije area. It was a building, small barracks, and a number of facilities around this. Any other military installations and where they were inside that complex, any warehouse or hangars, I don't know. But when you say the JNA, they are referring to the Zarko Zgonjanin barracks, as far as their facilities and installations, especially military installations are concerned, those were not public issues, and I do not know the exact location of the warehouse. It certainly was in Prijedor but whether in the Zarko Zgonjanin barracks or in the adjacent facilities or in Urije, or in a different place, I do not know that, nor was I particularly interested in that. It was publicly said that weapons had been withdrawn and transferred to the central warehouse and that it was under the supervision of the JNA. That was also a generally known fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With respect to that, is it fair to state, sir, that indeed the civilians, either the local, at the republic level or at the federal level had no authority or responsibility in respect to securing those barracks and military central depot in Prijedor. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was a JNA facility run by the army, commanded by the army. Only civilians were mobilised into the TO for the purpose of army drill, military drills, only in such situations could they be within the barracks. With which authorities exactly and with which duties, that was completely up to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And similarly, sir, the police whether at the republic level, the regional level, or the local level had absolutely no control and did not secure any of the premises involving the central depot or barracks in Prijedor from 1990, November, through approximately March of 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're asking me whether the police secured these military facilities. I don't know. I do know, however, that there was some form of cooperation after the takeover between the military and the police. But specifically, I'm not familiar with the form this cooperation took because I did not witness this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that not having witnessed it and telling us that you don't know what form this cooperation, if any, took, you are unable to share with us any information or any knowledge that you may have with respect to any interlinkage between the military or the police. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which period are you referring to, sir? Please, if you could just Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. specify.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The exact period you gave me in your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you talking about the period in 1992, from April on?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think that's the period you were referring to, sir, although my questions were confined to a period prior to that, your answer, and I think you shared with us, if I'm not correct, a period after that. So I'm just following up on your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I remember exactly you asked me about those relationships in the period prior to the elections where the warehouses were, what was returned, when whatever was returned was returned, so there was a procedure. There were certain authorities. And then after the takeover, at a later stage, after the takeover by the SDS, things began to change thoroughly and began to look very different. If your question is whether I entered the Zarko Zgonjanin barracks and whether I saw anything there, I never entered those facilities, and I do not know who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, it's clear now to me, I think. Did you, as a member of the Chamber of Municipalities at the republic level, representing Prijedor, were you under any mandate to follow the instructions and policy of the SDA party of which you were a member of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Parties established their policy before they enter parliament, and then through the legal parliamentary procedure, they implement this policy. And then once the party has established the vectors of activity, we carry out the decisions of this parliament, that is, of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And that's exactly what we did. There is another set of questions. If talking about problems of the local government, related to the municipal parliament, the distribution of power, or other regulations to be harmonised at the Municipal Assembly level, at the local level, then these local issues must be discussed at the local assembly and must be implemented by the local government.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Earlier this afternoon, we discussed Mr. Cehajic a little bit. And you shared with us what his duties and obligations, if you will, were, subsequent to the election of November 1990. And I understand that as president of the Municipal Assembly of the Prijedor municipality. Isn't it true, sir, that in fact any power, if any, that Mr. Cehajic had can only come through passage of legislation by the actual Municipal Assembly? He did not have any power separate from that which can be derived or given to him through passage of legislation within that Municipal Assembly. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The position of the president of municipality and his competencies are determined by the existing regulations down to the very last detail. So there was no need to invent what he could do and what he couldn't. His position, his function, was very clear. As well as that of the head of the municipal government and of other municipal departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that if the late Mr. Cehajic wanted to remove the military units that we were discussing as the hypothetical was, in the Prijedor municipality, he could not and had absolutely no power whatsoever to even attempt to remove that military unit without, first, placing it on the agenda of the Municipal Assembly of the Prijedor Municipality; second, having a vote, and he could only act upon whatever decision, either consistent with his view as to whether the military unit can stay, or adverse to his view, all he can do was implement that decision from the Municipal Assembly. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dear sir, I'm afraid I find myself compelled to repeat a number of things. The position of the JNA is not -- was not a municipal local issue. The position of the JNA, or parts of the JNA, is an issue dealt with at the republic level, through the existing institutions. Should there be a refusal to implement the authorities of the republic at the local level, then it is the obligation of the president of the municipal government or the president of the municipality to intervene with those departments refusing to implement the decisions that had been adopted at the republic level. Therefore, in no case was the issue of the JNA at the local level a local issue. According to the then-existing legislation, views were taken at the republic level regarding these issues. And then through the ministries, orders were implemented, and views were adopted, as concerned the local level. The violation of those decisions implied or entailed a violation of the laws of the republic. Failure to comply with these orders was failure to comply with the laws of the republic. At the same time, the implementation of some other decisions not adopted at the republic level meant for the local level to assume the competencies of the state, which is also against the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Was the military a republic institution or a federal institution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The military was a federal institution, but the authorities to command the army were evenly distributed throughout the republics, according to the existing law, the influence on the JNA was diametrically opposite. All the institutions in the republics had to be in a position to effect the work and the activities of the JNA because that was the army of all the republics, so it was a two-way street.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And let's, if we may, or if we can, the other day you discussed the atmosphere of change that occurred as a result of the SDA policy after the November 1990 elections. Again, I'm generally summarising that issue, so we want to discuss that to keep it in context.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm listening.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to that issue, do you have a position, sir, as to whether or not the party of the SDA contributed, in any way whatsoever, to this atmosphere of change after the November 1990 elections?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which changes are you referring to, if you could just please specify. You said the atmosphere of change, which atmosphere exactly are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm referring, sir, to the same atmosphere of change that you mentioned that resulted from purported SDS policy after November 1990 elections.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand. You mean the atmosphere between the SDA and the SDS. So your question was whether we, in any way, contributed to that atmosphere. As far as your question is concerned, a question you deal with directly or indirectly, the SDA, in no way, complicated the relationships in a wider context, that is, in Yugoslavia. We monitored the events. And at first, we advocated the preservation of Yugoslavia. It was a very delicate issue. Speaking of the pre-electoral period, we also talked about Yugoslavia. I think I said something to the effect yesterday. But there was a general change in atmosphere when two of the republics decided to secede. So that was one element contributing to this change in atmosphere. And another very important element was the propaganda in terms of media and in terms of military propaganda coming from Serbia, and then later on the war in Croatia. What I'm talking about here are very important facts, and it is in view of these facts that there was the SDA in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the SDS. The situation developed in such a way that, in a manner of speaking, the SDS forgot all about Bosnia and Herzegovina and decided to take sides, which meant to establish a state of their own that would remain within Yugoslavia. The wider context, the more general context, clearly demonstrated that this was not the best solution for Bosnia and Herzegovina. Negotiations were held, discussions were held, different initiatives were offered, but to no avail.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You state on page 19 of your June 12th, 2002, transcript -- I'd be happy to read the entire -- well, I will read it, from page 7 , your answer, if I may. And I have a couple questions on that answer. Again, line 7, page 19: "Answer: Many changes occurred. Compared to the atmosphere which reigned before the elections and at the time of the agreements on the possible coalitions prior to the elections, the main focus of our party, and this is something that we have heard from other political parties as well, was to defeat the communists. That was the main objective of our political party, and we had full support to that effect. And we endeavoured to take part in the process that had already started in eastern Europe. However, immediately after the elections, we were faced with the situation in which the SDS had completely different plans. They were not satisfied with simply defeating the communists; they started expressing certain aspirations which threatened to disrupt the relations with other political parties." My question to you, sir, is did the SDA, after the elections of 1990, have completely different plans than those that were announced in the pre-election platform? The SDA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Part of the elements of the pre-electoral campaign changed, which was dictated by the circumstances, the war in Croatia, the transgression of their constitutional competencies and authorities by the JNA, and the departure from Yugoslavia of two of its republics. So the SDA no longer thought this was Yugoslavia, but rather, that we were facing a situation where the arrangement on Yugoslavia needed to be renegotiated. And as far as I can remember, the SDA was ready to embark on that. However, even at that point, in certain situations, it became clear that the SDS had quite different ambitions. If you like, I can provide a very specific example.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sure we're going to get to that. But again, it's the pleasure of the Court and you. I don't want to interrupt you. I'll let you answer it, I guess. Sorry, if you'd like to answer, you may, or if you'd like to proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you want to have a specific example?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd love it, but perhaps if it's okay with you, we could wait until we come to that point. Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's all right. I agree. Do as you see fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to try to do what -- I've tried to establish a time line or a timetable with the events following the election of November 1990. So hopefully, we're done with pre-election discussions here. And just so that we have these timetables, I'm going to ask you, having been a member of the republic assembly and the chamber of municipalities, I want to know if you can help me understand and appreciate some of these dates.. We're going to come back to each section hopefully. All I want to do is establish this timetable for the moment. But if necessary, and if you would like, you can obviously answer the question in any manner that you see fit. You mentioned the change or circumstances dictating change following the elections. Do you know, sir, if the circumstances one month following the elections, namely, on December 22nd, 1990, that the Croatian Assembly passed a new coalition or a new constitution for the Republic of Croatia, which was the so-called Bozicni Ustav when the Croatians declared themselves as the National State of Croatian People and set forth within their constitution that the Serbs were to be considered not equal, as they were prior, but simply as a minority class. My question to you, sir, is were you aware that this event transpired on or about December 22nd, 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Was I aware that this event transpired? Yes, the media covered this, and that was after Croatia seceded from Yugoslavia. That was quite evident. What exactly the constitution or its provisions said, I did not look into that at that time. What I was interested in was Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as of course the local situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just so the date's approximately correct, right, December 22nd, 1990, to the best of your recollection? Right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the date. But as far as the wording is concerned, I can't say anything for sure. I can't confirm or deny. The fact is that Croatia did secede. First the League of Communists broke -- disintegrated, and Slovenia decided to secede and was followed by Croatia. And the general standpoint of both Slovenia and Croatia and perhaps this might be a useful piece of information for this Court, the general standpoint regardless of the internal legislation was that both of these republics were, at that point, prepared to discuss a new solution. And as we all remember, no doubt, and perhaps you had come across materials to this effect, both the president of Croatia and that of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the president of Macedonia met on several occasions during that period regardless of the developments in internal politics. So it was a stage at which negotiations were underway, on a general level.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: My next date for this timetable that I'm trying to establish, and to keep the atmosphere that we discussed prior to this line of questioning into a clearer context for myself, December 23rd, 1990, the Republic of Slovenia held a plebiscite. Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that the procedure in Slovenia was very much like that in Croatia. I can't remember the chronology, but what I've said before, and if you keep on asking me this, I will just repeat what I know. Both Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Slovenia and Croatia changed their internal legislation and became separate republics. That's separate from Yugoslavia. They participated in negotiations on a new solution for Yugoslavia. At times, it seemed as though the negotiations were to be successful, but the negotiations went on. They continued, and these were the most important news reported by all the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: December 26th, 1990. The Republic of Slovenia holds a referendum. Are you familiar with whether or not that date, December 26th, 1990, is accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know when exactly Slovenia was to hold a referendum. But I know that it did secede from Yugoslavia. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if it seceded from Yugoslavia in 1990 or in 1991, or any other time that you may think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that it was the first to secede, and then was followed by Croatia. I think that was the chronology. Whether they continued to participate in the federal institutions, they still tolerated the existence and activities of the JNA in their territory and those were the facts. I repeat, the negotiations continued as to the future and the new solutions for Yugoslavia and to find a way out of the crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me this, sir, when was the war in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the war in Slovenia broke out, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't say for sure. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, when the war broke out in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: War in Croatia broke out about mid-1991. I'm not sure really, but I think it was about that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now we're moving into 1991. So let's focus on that. On February 27th, 1991, as a member of the Chamber of Municipalities at the republic level, do you recall, sir, whether the SDA party, in that month on that day during that year, for the first time attempted to place an item on the agenda which was to seek a discussion on the independence and sovereignty and secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I can tell you is that I don't remember the exact dates of these sessions, and I'm speaking quite sincerely now. But I know that there was a whole number of questions connected to the breakup of Yugoslavia which had to be placed on the parliament's agenda. There were attempts to harmonise these different agendas. The SDS tried to dodge these problems or tried to impose certain issues to be placed on the agenda that were not acceptable for the other parties, the SDA, the HDZ, and the socialists, the communists, the reformists, and so on. The most serious problems occurred in the period I am talking about. There was no consensus regarding the intervention by the JNA in Slovenia. And there was no consensus about the use of force, about the changes in the federal organs. I can't remember exactly, but I know that there were changes in the federal organs at that time that were not interpreted as constitutional in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is a legal issue. And there were clear differences between the SDS, the viewpoints of the SDS, and the viewpoints of the other parties. So when these issues were concerned, mostly on one the side you had the SDS and the Serbian Radical Party, and all the other parties in the parliament on the opposite side. I remember that there were discussions concerning the federal budget, the competencies of the army. I can't remember the details, but it should be possible to find transcripts of these sessions and see what exactly was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Based upon your recollection, sir, isn't it true that less than three months from the November 1990 election, that the SDA party proposed that the item on the agenda at the republic assembly be added in order to have a discussion of the secession, sovereignty, and independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Within three months, do you remember that occurring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I can't remember exactly when. I repeat, because you've asked me before. And another thing, how to define exactly what happened, some said it was an attempt at secession. That was the SDS and Serbian Radical Party view. That's not how the other parties in the Bosnia-Herzegovina parliament perceived it. They tried to accept the state of facts and see in its true light the -- what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As you sit here, can you give us your best estimate of approximately how soon after the November 1990 elections did the SDA party make that proposition to seek the independence, sovereignty, and secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the former Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm, but can I at this stage intervene. Giving of evidence is not supposed to be a test of memory for the witness. If counsel has documents he wants to put to the witness, showing the dates, then he ought to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: All I'm asking his witness for is his best recollection of the events. When the Defence case proceeds, we will present that evidence as concrete. I don't want to have the witness testify on documents that we necessarily have at this time. If he doesn't remember the date, and he can't give us an approximate date, then that's all the witness has to tell me. I truly just wanted to go through the timeline in a quicker order. But I'm reluctant to interrupt, respectfully, the witness if he has something to add on this point, although I plan to cover each point in some detail, not as exhaustive as perhaps others would like. All I'm asking for is an approximate date to the best of his recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. If, in principle, the witness could answer a little bit shorter, probably just yes or no when the questions of this kind arise. On the other hand, it has to be understood that it's fair to try to put all the developments in the former Yugoslavia in context, and then, as I understood correctly, in the context of Prijedor. I think this line of questioning, therefore, the submission -- the objection is dismissed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the third time, I can tell you the following: I don't remember on which date which decision was proposed because there was a huge number of sessions. Sometimes we were sitting for 10 or 15 days in a row, and it lasted for several months, and now you're asking me to remember whether a specific decision was adopted on a specific date. I would be really happy to be able to give you an answer, but I was not in a position to follow the proceedings that closely. The parliament was very often in session, and a huge number of issues were on the agenda. So once again, if you want a simple answer, no, I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know if, in September of 1991, there was a mobilisation of men issued by the SFRY for the area and territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you referring to the Yugoslav People's Army? I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, whether or not there was a second mobilisation call in November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, federal organs, therefore, including the JNA, whenever they issued a mobilisation call, the federal command would address this call or order to the leadership in the -- of the republic. The republic leadership would then adopt a position on that and transmit the order to lower levels of authority. When the BH leadership received an order from a federal institution -- when the BH leadership received such an order from a federal institution, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if, at any time in November or thereabouts of 1991, a new coalition was formed between the party of the SDA and the party of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No coalition between the SDA and HDZ was ever formed. If that had been the case, I would have been aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did, sir, in fact, in November of 1991, the HDZ and the SDA vote together to put the issue of sovereignty, independence, and secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the agenda in the assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That decision was voted by seven or eight political parties. Therefore, by all parties with the exception of the SDS and the Serb Radical Party. So the entire opposition, all of the left-wing parties which included members of all ethnicities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, HDZ and SDA, that is, without the SDS and the Serb Radical Party, which means the rest of the parliament which had a sufficient number of deputies to have a quorum to do that, and involved members, deputies, of all ethnicities including Serbs. You limited your question only to the SDA and the HDZ, but for the purposes of clarity, I'm telling you that other political parties also participated in the adoption of this decision. This decision was voted with the majority of votes with very few -- with very few abstentions. It was almost a unanimous decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And this happened around November of 1991, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And this happened, sir, in approximately November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible that it was in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, sir, when the assembly in the republic level passed a memorandum on the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it was in early 1992. I'm not sure, either in late February or early March 1992, but I'm not sure. I do not remember clearly the date. But at any rate, it was in early 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: A couple months before the incidents that occurred in April of 1992. Would that be a fair way to summarise it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Chronologically speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's all I'm trying to do is chronologically get these dates. We'll discuss them hopefully at some length. Also in November 1991, sir, was an entity called a Conference on European Security and Cooperation, namely the CESC present in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time, November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is, European monitors were present at the parliament. They attended the parliament session, mostly in twos, sometimes only one would attend. But there would always be someone. I don't know what kind of presence they had elsewhere on the ground, but I remember clearly that they were present at the parliament sessions. We used to call them monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And sir, I think during your direct examination, you were provided a document which reflected a minutes of meetings from the Prijedor Municipal Assembly from February 14th, 1992. And you were at that meeting. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you have please the document? I think it's not possible for the witness to recollect the exact date of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't produce that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's quite right. But on the basis of this document, you shall answer a question. It's better to have the document present for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At this moment --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he wasn't present at the 14th of February assembly. It was one of the documents he was going to look at but it wasn't actually shown to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I misspoke that it was shown, I know at great length we discussed it. In any event I'll move on from that. And if I may finish just this chronology, and -- I want to thank the usher, I apologize. We'll get back to that, because it's -- I have some questions on that meeting, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Five more minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know if on February 29th, 1992, and March 1st, 1992, approximately two months before the events that unfolded in the Prijedor Municipality, that, in fact, a referendum on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina was held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The referendum was called before that -- I'm trying to remember the date, but it escapes me. But you are right, it was called prior to these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On April 8th, 1992, sir, do you know if there was an order from the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina regarding mobilisation which came directly from the republic level, indicating the callup of mobilisation of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that a callup of mobilisation of the Territorial Defence took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but do you know if it occurred on or about April 8th, 1992, less than three weeks from the events that unfolded in Prijedor on April Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 30th of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know it did occur, and I know that in Prijedor, we talked to the SDS and tried to implement the decision which was adopted at the republic level. But I also know that at that time, it was already almost impossible to talk to the SDS. They had already established the Serb Municipality of Prijedor, as early as January.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When, sir, did you find it difficult to address any issues with the SDS? When was the time period at which you felt that the communications between the SDA, and specifically yourself, had completely broken down vis-a-vis the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a certain level of communication up until the end of April, 1992, that is, until the takeover. There was communication on several occasions even after that. Now, if you're asking me about the time period when the communications became difficult, I think we have to go back to the period of time when the power was being divided and when first disagreements occurred. Later, the attitude of the SDS towards the republic institutions became very complicated because the SDS did not take over some of the municipal -- did not manage to take over some of the municipal departments and was accusing the SDA because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just one last question before the break: What time did this happen that you felt it was impossible for the communications to proceed? What time period? 1991, 1992? And if you can tell us -- if you don't recall, please share that with us as well -- when in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you, immediately after the elections, the communication was good. The top positions were divided in a regular fashion. However, in the following period, when other positions were being distributed, the situation became exacerbated. When orders came from the republic level, the SDS officials obstructed the implementation of these orders. That, too, created difficulties. A rift occurred, and when the federal army attempted to mobilise the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina, while the leadership of Bosnia and Herzegovina had a different attitude -- they were against the war in Croatia, whereas the SDS was in favour of the war in Croatia -- that added further to the disagreements. I'm talking about 1991. When aspirations became apparent for the regionalisation, the problems got worse. When the SDS proclaimed 70 per cent of the territory of the Prijedor Municipality as Serb, then the communication became virtually impossible. In view of the circumstances, it was clear that attempts were being made to implement something that had already been implemented and carried out in certain other areas. It all culminated in the takeover by the SDS through military means which rendered all the communications impossible. The SDS adopted a peremptory position towards all others and towards us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stands adjourned until 5 minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, if I may continue with some more questions on this time line, April 30th, 1992, the takeover of Prijedor occurred. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May 1st, 1992, the day after the takeover, you came to Prijedor and actually you met with fellow members of the SDA party in your party headquarters or offices. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With some of the members of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Right. May 15th through the 16th -- strike that. Mid-May 1992, approximately, according to your testimony that you provided, you and representatives of the SDA had a meeting with the SDS party. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. Sometime in mid-May. I cannot be more precise. Several days before that or after, but it was at that time that we had this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And sometime in May 1992, you also had a meeting with various members of the SDA in Kozarac. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. May --
